subject: First-token SLOs & streaming choices for Nimbus Payments

From: Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.com>

Subject: First-token SLOs & streaming choices for Nimbus Payments

Alex — thanks again for a focused call earlier. Quick recap + proposed next steps so we’re aligned before the tech deep dive:

Summary of customer goals (from call):
- Mobile checkout UX requires fast perceived response; target first token for short prompts (checkout prompts) is sub-120ms ideally (measured from request arrival at edge to client-received first chunk).
- Peak scenario: 20 requests/sec sustained across region; concurrency up to 400 active sessions (mobile + web); burst up to 500r/s expected during promotions.
- Streaming required for conversational confirmation flow; mobile SDK would prefer WebSocket to reduce RTT overhead; web clients would be fine with SSE.

Initial SLO proposal (see attached SLO-proposal-v1.pdf):
- First-token target: <= 150ms P50, aim for <= 120ms P90 for core checkout flow (we flagged your preference for 100–120ms and set an actionable target).
- Streaming channels: recommend WebSocket for mobile app (lower handshake overhead, persistent connection), SSE for web (simplicity, auto-reconnect).
- Chunk cadence: suggest 100–180ms chunk cadence for 10–20 token chunks for responsive UX without overwhelming client buffers.
- Throughput sizing: see capacity-estimate.xlsx attached — ballpark: 8 dedicated GPUs (quantized model) with autoscale headroom to handle bursts.

Immediate asks / next steps:
1) Can you confirm whether the 120ms P90 target is a hard requirement or a stretch goal?
2) Please confirm which clients will use WebSocket vs SSE (mobile vs web) so we can tune connection strategy.
3) Procurement contact: include procurement (procurement@nimbus-payments.com) on email so we can start MSA/PO conversations; I’ve attached the SLO draft to speed review.
4) Proposed tech deep dive: Tue Mar 24, 10am PT — Marcus and I will demo a streaming proof-of-concept and go through chunk cadence experiments. Are you available?

Thanks — I’ll slot time for the deep dive once we get confirmation.

— Laura Bennett

Laura — thanks for the write-up, this is helpful. A few clarifications from our side: 

- The 120ms P90 is aspirational for the mobile checkout path; procurement and security will want a more conservative guaranteed SLO (we can take 150ms to contract and a 120ms target in the SLA appendix). So: hard requirement for contract = 150ms P90, product goal = 120ms P90.
- Confirming client mapping: mobile SDK (iOS/Android) -> WebSocket; Web portal -> SSE. Internal tools (ops dashboard) won't stream.
- Curious about buffering: our mobile SDK buffers up to 200ms by default to smooth jitter. If you deliver very small chunks at 100ms cadence, the UX benefit might not be observed unless we reduce client-side buffering. Can your demo run two cadence profiles so we can see end-to-end perceived latency?
- Procurement copied. We’d like a short (2–3 page) appendix that spells out failure modes & fallbacks for streaming (e.g., model fallback, JSON framing, reconnection behavior) for legal/security review.

We are available Tue Mar 24, 10am PT for the tech deep dive. Please include Marcus for the kernel/execution details.

Thanks,
Alex Park

Hi Alex / Laura — quick engineering read on the proposal and what we should demo on Tue: 

- WebSocket vs SSE: both supported by Redwood. WebSocket reduces RTT in mobile scenarios because it avoids repeated HTTP handshakes and lets us push the first chunk immediately after generation. SSE is simpler for browsers (no persistent binary framing). We should show both.
- Chunk cadence tradeoffs: smaller chunks (50–100ms cadence) improve perceived responsiveness but increase total number of frames and CPU/network overhead. Given your mobile client buffer (~200ms), I suggest testing 120ms and 180ms cadences in the demo — these bracket your expected client behavior.
- First-token sources of latency: network (CDN + mobile cellular), TLS handshake (mitigated by persistent WS), model decode + kernel scheduling. Our runtime tuning options: shorter KV cache prefetch windows, aggressive continuous batching for throughput paths, and kernel prioritization for checkout prompt class.
- Sizing note: capacity-estimate.xlsx is conservative. For a quantized Llama-derivative at your mix and P90 targets, 6–8 A100-class equivalents with autopinning + burst policy should meet 150ms P90; to hit 120ms P90 reliably across AZs we recommend 8–10 with regional redundancy.
- Failure/fallbacks appendix: we can provide a concise appendix covering: model fallback (smaller quantized variant), connection fallback (WS -> SSE -> chunked polling), and graceful degradation (shorter responses + offer to fall back to cached static responses). See attached chunking-playbook.md for the cadence tests I’ll run in the demo.

I’ll run an initial cadence experiment and attach results during the call.

— Marcus
Senior SRE, Redwood Inference
marcus.lin@redwood.com

Agreed SLOs & channels:
- Contracted SLO: First-token <= 150ms P90 (US region).
- Product objective: First-token <= 120ms P90 for mobile checkout flow (tracked in the SLO appendix).
- Streaming: Mobile -> WebSocket; Web -> SSE. Marcus will instrument two chunk cadences in the demo (120ms, 180ms).
- Client buffering note: Nimbus will evaluate reducing mobile SDK buffer from 200ms to 100ms for the checkout flow; Redwood will run cadence tests to show perceived improvements.
